title: Ray Gun, premiere issue
lede: The first issue of the music magazine Ray Gun, November 1992: painted and scratched covers, typewriter lists, and spreads where text is layered until it turns into texture.
summary: Scratched yellow cover with a red condensed masthead, typewriter band list, and overprinted, collaged spreads inside. David Carson, Ray Gun no. 1, 1992.

source.label: Display Graphic Design Collection: Ray Gun, Premiere Issue, November 1992

evidence.note: Inspected eight photographs (1600 × 1279 each) of one copy offered by Display, a design collection and bookshop, in scratchpad copies: the cover, six interior spreads, and one further collaged page with the masthead. The copy has no collection number. Not stored.

styles.note: Clear example: the first issue of the magazine that defines the style, with scratched, overprinted, and hand-lettered type over painted and photocopied grounds.

context: Ray Gun was a music magazine first published in Santa Monica in 1992, with Marvin Scott Jarrett as publisher and David Carson as art director. Wikipedia describes its editorial pages as a “chaotic, abstract ‘grunge typography’ style”. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Gun_(magazine)).

Display lists the issue as no. 1, November 1992, 10 × 12 inches, 100 pages, with Carson credited as design consultant. Its first page reads “Raw by choice. Immediate by necessity. Alternative by design.” [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/ray-gun-premiere-issue-november-1992-david-carson).

Features include Henry Rollins, Sonic Youth (photographed by Spike Jonze), The Lemonheads, and The Prodigy. [Display](https://bookstore.thisisdisplay.org/products/ray-gun-premiere-issue-november-1992-david-carson).
observed: The cover is a scraped yellow, white, and black painted surface with pencil scrawl, paint spatter, and a heavy black scribble.
Two black-and-white face fragments are cut into rough rectangles and pasted into the paint.

The masthead “rAY GUn” is a red condensed sans-serif in mixed case, with letters of different heights; “PREMIERE ISSUE” is blue hand lettering; the band list is a typewriter face, indented in an uneven zigzag.
The Sonic Youth opener layers strips of contact-sheet film, overprinted serif and sans-serif lines, and blue text until lines collide.
A second Sonic Youth spread has large blue hand-painted words over a page of body text, facing a painted face on red gingham with a scrawled title.
One spread overprints lines of text in several faces until the headline area becomes a solid black mass.
A music-video feature sets its body in a condensed typewriter face, justified in narrow columns, facing a cropped blue duotone photograph.
Headlines break words across lines and space them down the page (“lov / i / ng / the / rock / star”).
interpretation: The issue shows the whole grammar at once: damaged grounds, several unrelated faces per spread, and body text used as a texture. The typewriter lists and captions are the stable voice among the noise.
borrow: Set a list of names in a typewriter face with alternating indents instead of a clean column.
Overprint a headline in several faces and colors until part of it becomes a black mass, and keep the body text clean beside it.
Paste photo fragments with rough rectangular edges onto a painted or scratched ground.

rights.statement: No image is stored. David Carson is living, so the design is in copyright. Photographs by their sources.
